row.description: Brittenburg was a Roman ruin site west of Leiden between Katwijk aan Zee and Noordwijk aan Zee, presumably identical to the even older Celtic Lugdunum fortress [1]. The site is first mentioned in 1401, was uncovered more completely by storm erosion in 1520, 1552 and 1562, and has subsequently been entirely eroded away [1]. When built, it was located at the mouth of the Oude Rijn (old river Rhine), which has since moved [1]. The site was about one kilometre west of the European Space Research and Technology Centre, now offshore in the North Sea [1]. The site, known as "Brittenburg", was still visible in the dunes in the fourteenth century, but the gradual advance of the sea made the ruins lie on the beach in the sixteenth and seventeenth century [1]. Today, they would be somewhere in the North Sea, inaccessible to archaeological research [1]. All that remains is a small set of finds, collected in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and a famous map by Ortelius [1].
row.card: Storm erosion uncovered more of the Roman ruin Brittenburg in 1520, 1552 and 1562, and it has since eroded away entirely. All that remains is a set of finds and a famous map by Ortelius.

row.description: The Pagans Hill Roman Temple was a Romano-British-style temple (Romano-Celtic temple) excavated on Pagans Hill at Chew Stoke in the English county of Somerset [1]. The temple faced east and was first built in the late-3rd century, possibly to the god Mercury [1]. After the collapse of the original building another temple was built, which again fell into ruin [1]. The final rebuild, after about 367 CE included the addition of an internal screen [1]. The temple was on a promontory overlooking the River Chew [1]. It was excavated by Philip Rahtz between 1949 and 1953 [1]. Among the artefacts found in the well approximately 15 meters west of the temple foundations, was an unusual sculpture of a dog with collar [1].
row.card: On a promontory above the River Chew, Pagans Hill Roman Temple faced east, possibly built for Mercury. A well about 15 meters west of its foundations held an unusual sculpture of a dog.

row.description: The El Brujo Archaeological Complex is an ancient archaeological site, located in the Chicama Valley just north of Trujillo, La Libertad Province, Peru, that was occupied from preceramic times [1]. Huaca Prieta is the earliest part of the complex but the biggest constructions on the site belong to the Moche culture [1]. In this area, there are also the remains of the later Lambayeque and Chimú cultures [1]. The Brujo Complex is represented by three major huacas [1]. The Huaca Prieta mound dates back to the preceramic times [1]. A 17th-century letter found during excavations at the site may contain translations of numbers written in Quingnam (sometimes known as Pescadora) using the decimal system, the first physical evidence for the existence of this language [1].
row.card: In the Chicama Valley, El Brujo's biggest constructions belong to the Moche. A 17th-century letter found at the site may contain translations of numbers written in Quingnam.

row.description: Kastelli Giant's Church is a prehistoric stone enclosure situated near Pattijoki in the North Ostrobothnia region of Finland [1]. It is one of the largest of forty such "Giant's Churches" to be found in this region of Finland [1]. It dates to around 2000 BC [1]. The Giant's Church at Kastelli is a rectangular stone enclosure measuring around 60 by 35 metres [1]. The walls are seven metres wide and survive to a height of two metres [1]. When built it would have been on a rocky shoreline [1]. The enclosure is surrounded by more than twenty stone cairns [1]. The site was excavated in the 1920s; it has been dated to around 2000 BC [1].
row.card: When built, Kastelli Giant's Church would have stood on a rocky shoreline: a stone enclosure of around 60 by 35 metres, its walls seven metres wide, ringed by more than twenty cairns.

row.description: Broch of Mousa or Mousa Broch is a preserved Iron Age broch or round tower [1]. It is on the island of Mousa in Shetland [1]. It is the tallest broch still standing and amongst the best-preserved prehistoric buildings in Europe [1]. It is thought to have been constructed c. 300 BC [1]. Mousa Broch continued to be used over the centuries and is mentioned in two Norse Sagas [1]. The Orkneyinga Saga gives an account of a siege of the broch by Earl Harald Maddadsson in 1153 following the abduction of his mother [1].
row.card: On Mousa in Shetland rises the Broch of Mousa, the tallest broch still standing. Thought built circa 300 BC, it was besieged by Earl Harald Maddadsson in 1153, says the Orkneyinga Saga.

row.description: Le Mormont is a hill in the Swiss canton of Vaud, part of the Éclépens municipality, about halfway between lakes Neuchatel and Geneva [1]. In 2009, the cantonal archaeological office of Vaud performed a watching brief excavation, which led to the discovery of a late La Tène period (c. 100 BC) Helvetic cult site with a total of 250 Celtic burial pits containing sacrificial deposits [1]. Among the deposited goods were ceramic and bronze vessels, iron tools, jewelry, grinding stones, coins, and both animal and human remains [1]. It was reported as being of unprecedented size and richness for the period [1]. It is unclear whether the human remains represent a cemetery or evidence of human sacrifice [1]. The site is of primary importance for Gaulish religion on the eve of the Roman conquest [1].
row.card: On Mormont, a hill in Vaud, a late La Tène cult site held pits filled with vessels, iron tools, jewelry, coins, animal and human remains. Reported as unprecedented in size and richness.

row.description: Nicopolis ad Istrum or Nicopolis ad Iatrum was a Roman and Early Byzantine town [1]. Its ruins are located at the village of Nikyup, 20 km north of Veliko Tarnovo in northern Bulgaria [1]. The town reached its zenith during the reigns of Hadrian, the Antonines and the Severan dynasty [1]. The city was founded by Trajan around 102–106 in memory of his victory in the Dacian Wars over the Roxolani and also later victories in 105 [1]. The monumental character of the city however dates mainly to Hadrian and Antoninus Pius and inscriptions found are no earlier than 136 when the name Ulpia Nicopolis ad Istrum was in use [1]. The classical town was planned according to the orthogonal system [1]. The agora contained a statue of Trajan on horseback as well as other marble statues and an Ionic colonnade [1]. The city also had a three-nave basilica, a bouleuterion, a temple of Cybele, a small odeon, thermae (public baths) as well as a unique Roman building inscribed with termoperiatos, a heated building with shops and enclosed space for walks and business meetings [1].
row.card: Trajan founded Nicopolis ad Istrum in memory of his Dacian Wars victory. Its agora held his statue on horseback, and the city had a heated building with shops and enclosed space for walks.

row.description: Cularo was the name of the Gallic city which evolved into modern Grenoble [1]. The earliest remaining reference to what is now Grenoble dates back to a July 43 BC letter written by Munatius Plancus to Cicero [1]. The small town founded by the Allobroges Gallic people was at that time called Cularo [1]. In 292, the western emperor Maximian elevated the town to the rank of Civitas, "city", and ordered the construction of defensive walls which both protected the urban area and marked its higher status [1]. Wishing to thank and honor the emperor Gratian for creating its bishopric, the inhabitants of Cularo renamed their town Gratianopolis in 381 [1]. That name would subsequently evolve into Grenoble through Graignovol [1]. Several small sections of the Gallo-Roman city wall are also visible in the old town [1].
row.card: Cularo, a town founded by the Allobroges, thanked the emperor Gratian for its bishopric by renaming itself Gratianopolis in 381. That name became Grenoble, where Gallo-Roman walls remain.

row.description: Rapidum was a Roman settlement and fort located in Mauretania Caesariensis, nearly 100 km south of Icosium (Algiers) [1]. Soon under Hadrian near the fort grew up a civilian settlement called "Rapidum", on the Roman road called the Nova Praetentura [1]. The original castrum of Rapidum remained until 201 AD, while the town survived until emperor Aurelian when it was destroyed by Berber nomads [1]. The initial garrison of Rapidum fort was – according to historian M. Ruiu – the Cohors II Sardorum and protected the new limes of the Roman Empire moved south from the Mediterranean shores to a military road called Nova Praetentura [1]. This road went from Rapidum near Numidia to Altava and to Numerus Syrorum at the border of Mauretania Tingitana [1]. Rapidum was named "municipium" and had an extension of 15 hectares under Marcus Aurelius (with nearly 4,000 inhabitants, mostly romanised Berbers, like Auzia) [1].
row.card: Nearly 100 km south of Algiers, a civilian settlement grew up near a Roman fort under Hadrian. Rapidum became a municipium with nearly 4,000 inhabitants under Marcus Aurelius.

row.description: Clausentum was a small town in the Roman province of Britannia [1]. The site is believed to be located in Bitterne Manor, which is now a suburb of Southampton [1]. The settlement is located on a promontory jutting into the River Itchen [1]. The first archaeological excavations were conducted in 1935, and Molly Cotton undertook excavations from 1951 to 1954 [1]. The excavations showed that it was the site of a small town in the 1st and 2nd centuries [1]. At a later date a stone defensive wall was erected around the site [1]. The early excavators dated the erection of this wall to around 370, but later evidence showed that the walls were erected around 280–90, at about the same time as the fort at nearby Portchester [1]. Four Roman milestones and three possible milestones were found at Bitterne between 1800 and 1850 [1].
row.card: Clausentum was a small town in Roman Britannia, later walled in stone around 280–90, at about the same time as the fort at nearby Portchester. Four Roman milestones were found at Bitterne.

row.description: Caterthun, or the Caterthuns, is a ridge of hills near the city of Brechin in Angus [1]. The Caterthuns are notable for being the site of two Iron Age forts known as the White Caterthun and the Brown Caterthun which are designated as a scheduled monument [1]. The White Caterthun, on the west, is dominated by an oval fort consisting of a massive dry-stone wall, with a well or cistern in the middle [1]. The light-coloured stone wall gives the White Caterthun its name [1]. The Brown Caterthun, on the east, consists of a series of earthen embankments [1]. There is little evidence of settlement, agriculture or water supply here, so the purpose of the earthworks is uncertain [1]. Both Caterthuns show several entrances to the summit that radiate outwards, like the spokes on a wheel [1]. From radio-carbon dating, the Brown Caterthun appears to have been built and modified over several centuries in the latter half of the first millennium BC [1].
row.card: On a ridge near Brechin, the Caterthuns hold two Iron Age forts: the White Caterthun, an oval fort of massive dry-stone wall, and the Brown Caterthun, a series of earthen embankments.

row.description: Pirak is an archaeological site belonging to the Indus Valley civilization located in Balochistan [1]. It is 20 km south of Sibi east of the Nari River [1]. The site of Pirak was first reported by Robert Raikes in 1963 [1]. It was excavated, between 1968 and 1974, before the well known sites of Mehrgarh or Nausharo by the French archaeological mission team led by Jean Marie Casal [1]. According to the excavator, this site was occupied from c.1800 BCE to 800 BCE [1]. The site has some very early ironwork and iron artefacts [1]. The excavator records three phases of unbroken occupation in Safi pirak [1]. The earliest indubitable evidence of domestic horse comes from Safi Pirak, during period I (c.1700 BC) [1].
row.card: In Balochistan, Pirak has some very early ironwork and iron artefacts. Its excavator dates the occupation from circa 1800 BCE to 800 BCE and records three phases of unbroken occupation.

row.description: The Lohra tomb was a megalithic monument outside Lohra near Marburg in north central Hesse, Germany [1]. It is one of the lesser known among its type in Central Europe [1]. It dates to the Late Neolithic, probably just after 3000 BC [1]. It belongs to the gallery graves of the Wartberg culture, but is unique among them because of its rich ceramic assemblage [1]. The tomb was discovered accidentally in 1931 by the farmer Jakob Elmshäuser who encountered an obstacle when ploughing a field [1]. The tomb consisted of a large main chamber and a small open antechamber [1]. In contrast to the finds from the well-known tombs at Züschen or Altendorf, the dead at Lohra had been cremated [1]. 20 vessels that had been placed on the chamber floor and later covered in human ashes were almost fully preserved [1].
row.card: In 1931 a farmer ploughing near Marburg encountered an obstacle: the Lohra Megalithic Tomb, a large main chamber with a small open antechamber, its dead cremated.

row.description: Often referred to as the "Pearl of the Black Sea", Nesebar is a rich city-museum defined by more than three millennia of ever-changing history [1]. The small city exists in two parts separated by a narrow human-made isthmus with the ancient part of the settlement on the peninsula [1]. The older part bears evidence of occupation by a variety of different civilisations over the course of its existence [1]. At 425-424 BC the town joined the Delian League, under the leadership of Athens [1]. Remains date mostly from the Hellenistic period and include the acropolis, a temple of Apollo and an agora [1]. A wall which formed part of the Thracian fortifications can still be seen on the north side of the peninsula [1].
row.card: Often called the Pearl of the Black Sea, Nesebar is a small city in two parts, its ancient part on a peninsula. Its remains include an acropolis, a temple of Apollo and an agora.

row.description: The Dipylon (Greek: Δίπυλον, "Two-Gated") was the main gate in the city wall of Classical Athens [1]. Located in the modern suburb of Kerameikos, it led to the namesake ancient cemetery [1]. The gate was of major ceremonial significance as the starting point of the procession of the Great Panathenaea, and accordingly it was a large, monumental structure [1]. Erected in 478 BC as part of Themistocles' fortification of Athens and rebuilt in the 300s BC, it remained standing and in use until the 3rd century AD [1]. The Dipylon was the "largest gate of the ancient world", with a surface of c. 1,800 square metres [1]. The original, Themistoclean-era gate largely established the final shape of the structure and covered the same area as the Hellenistic structure, and was built of clay bricks on top of a pedestal of Poros limestone blocks [1]. The Hellenistic gate complex was an altogether more massive and elaborate affair, being built of large finely hewn ashlar blocks [1]. The northern cityward gate is still visible, but the southern one has been destroyed through the construction of a modern canal [1].
row.card: The Dipylon, the Two-Gated, was the main gate of Classical Athens, where the procession of the Great Panathenaea began. Erected in 478 BC, it was rebuilt in the 300s BC.

row.description: The Vätteryd grave field, also known as Vätterydshed, is an Iron Age grave field in Hässleholm Municipality in Scania, Sweden [1]. The site is located in a heathfield between the localities of Tjörnarp and Sösdala [1]. Between 1955 and 1957, an archaeological survey was made of part of the burial ground [1]. The grave goods found — including bronze jewelry, glass and bronze pearls, and bronze wire — were taken to various museums in Stockholm [1].
row.card: Between Tjörnarp and Sösdala lies the Vätteryd Grave Field, an Iron Age burial ground that gave up bronze jewelry, glass and bronze pearls, silver threads and silver bands.

row.description: Wilcahuaín, Willcahuaín, or Huilcahuaín is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is located near the village of Paria, 6 km northeast of the city of Huaraz, Ancash; at an elevation of 3,400 m (11,200 ft) [1]. Wilcahuaín is regarded as one of the most important archaeological sites of the Wari culture [1]. It was possibly built ca. 1100 AD [1].
row.card: Near the village of Paria, 6 km northeast of Huaraz in Ancash and 3,400 m up, stands Wilcahuaín, regarded as one of the most important archaeological sites of the Wari culture.

row.description: The Pilgrims' Way is the historical route supposedly taken by pilgrims from Winchester in Hampshire, England, to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury in Kent [1]. This name, of comparatively recent coinage, is applied to a pre-existing ancient trackway dated by archaeological finds to 600–450 BC, but probably in existence since the Stone Age [1]. The prehistoric route followed the "natural causeway" east to west on the southern slopes of the North Downs [1]. The prehistoric trackway extended further than the present Way, providing a link from the narrowest part of the English Channel to the important religious complexes of Avebury and Stonehenge, in Wiltshire, where it is known as the Harroway [1]. The way then existed as "broad and ill-defined corridors of movement up to half a mile wide" and not as a single, well-defined track [1]. The route was still followed as an artery for through traffic in Roman times [1].
row.card: The Pilgrims' Way, supposedly taken by pilgrims from Winchester to Thomas Becket's shrine at Canterbury, is a comparatively recent name for an ancient trackway dated by finds to 600–450 BC.

row.description: Stoke Hill is a large hill rising to the north of Exeter in Devon, England [1]. It is significant as the site of both an Iron Age hill fort and a later Roman signal station [1]. The hill fort is situated slightly below and northeast of the Roman signal station, putting it in a better position to have sight of a number of other hill forts simultaneously [1]. It is at an elevation of approximately 145 metres above sea level [1]. The signal station is at the highest point of the hill, 159 metres above sea level [1].
row.card: North of Exeter, a Roman signal station crowns Stoke Hill, 159 metres above sea level; slightly below, an Iron Age hill fort is placed to sight a number of other hill forts at once.

row.description: Sagaholm is the site of Bronze Age burial mounds (Sagaholmshögen) [1]. Sagaholm is located in Ljungarums parish just south of Jönköping in Småland, Sweden [1]. Sagaholmshögen is a cairn dating from the early Nordic Bronze Age (c. 1700–500 BC) [1]. The site had a large barrow with a circle of slabs of sandstone, probably numbering as many as 100 [1]. Only 45 graves remain, with 18 of them adorned with petroglyphs depicting ships, animals and people [1].
row.card: Just south of Jönköping, the Bronze Age barrow of Sagaholm was ringed by sandstone slabs, probably as many as 100. Of the slabs that remain, 15 are carved with ships, animals and people.

row.description: Tal-Barrani contains a significant number of archaeological remains [1]. These include an ancient tomb cluster and field systems at the Tal-Ħotba site at Tal-Barrani, and a number of late Roman and Byzantine catacombs [1]. Three ancient Punic rock-cut tombs were uncovered and investigated by the Museums Department in 1965 and 1966 in the Tal-Ħotba area of Tal-Barrani [1]. The tombs were uncovered during the construction of a milk depot on previously undeveloped agricultural land [1]. In May 1993, an important Late Roman to Byzantine burial site was uncovered during trenching works along Tal-Barrani road [1]. Two subterranean burial monuments were discovered within 10.0 metres from each other [1]. These were a multi-chambered burial catacomb, and a Late Roman rock-cut chamber tomb [1].
row.card: Three Punic rock-cut tombs came to light at Tal-Barrani during the building of a milk depot. In May 1993, trenching uncovered a multi-chambered catacomb and a Late Roman chamber tomb.

row.description: Dewerstone is the site of an Iron Age Hill fort on a rocky promontory overlooking the River Plym on the South West edge of Dartmoor to the North of Plympton in Devon [1]. The fort consists of ramparts to the Northern side of the promontory at approx 210 Metres above Sea Level [1]. "Dewer" is an ancient Celtic word for the Devil, and Dartmoor tradition has it that the Devil gallops across the Moor each night and leads a phantom pack of black hounds to chase weary or foolish humans over the Dewerstone to their deaths [1].
row.card: Dewerstone is a rocky promontory above the River Plym with hill fort ramparts. Dartmoor tradition says the Devil's phantom black hounds chase the weary or foolish over it to their deaths.

row.description: The Duddo Five Stones is a stone circle north of Duddo in North Northumberland, approximately 4 miles South of the Scottish Border [1]. The stones were known as the Four Stones until 1903, when the fifth stone was re-erected to improve the skyline [1]. There were originally seven stones, the empty sockets of two stones being found on the western side during excavation in the 1890s [1]. The stones are formed of a local soft pink Doddington sandstone [1]. The site of the Duddo Stones offers panoramic views of the Cheviot Hills to the South and the Lammermuir Hills to the north [1]. The location was the subject of an archeological investigation in 2008 [1].
row.card: Of soft pink sandstone, the Duddo Five Stones look out over the Cheviot and Lammermuir Hills. Known as the Four Stones until 1903, when the fifth was re-erected to improve the skyline.

row.description: La Tène is a protohistoric archaeological site on the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel [1]. Dating to the second part of the European Iron Age it is the type site of the La Tène culture, which dates to about 450 BCE to the 1st century BCE and extends from Ireland to Anatolia and from Portugal to Czechia [1]. The site is located in the lieu-dit La Tène [1]. It is also the point where the Thielle river leaves the lake and flows in the direction of lake Biel [1]. The site of La Tène was discovered in 1857 during a period dubbed the "lake dwelling fever" [1]. In November 1857, fisherman Hans Kopp was sailing to a Neolithic dwelling near Concise from Lake Biel under orders from Colonel Friedrich Schwab when he spotted an interesting spot near La Tène [1]. He stopped and started investigating, and within an hour he had found around forty iron objects, among which were eight spearheads and twelve swords [1]. Around 1870, the first Jura water correction brought the lake level 2.7 m lower, and the site which was believed to be exhausted proved to have more to be found [1].
row.card: On Lake Neuchâtel's northern shore lies La Tène, the type site of the La Tène culture. Around 1870 the lake fell 2.7 m, and a site believed to be exhausted proved to have more to be found.

row.description: Wet Withens is a Bronze Age henge on Eyam Moor in the Derbyshire Peak District [1]. On gritstone moorland over 300 metres above sea level, the site has clear views of the valley of the River Derwent and Higger Tor [1]. The earthen bank of Wet Withens is over 30m in diameter, making it the largest embanked stone circle in Derbyshire [1]. The 'Chair Stone' is the tallest and most prominent stone with a ledge cut out of its face, appearing as a seat [1]. About 10m north of the henge is a large stone cairn (known as Eyam Moor Barrow) about 27m long and 1m high [1]. Near the middle of the cairn is an unusual cup-marked stone [1]. The cairn's shape indicates that it was likely to have been a prehistoric burial barrow [1]. Wet Withens is also known as Eyam Moor 1 because there are 2 smaller stone circles about 650m to the east [1].
row.card: On Eyam Moor, with clear views of the River Derwent valley, Wet Withens is the largest embanked stone circle in Derbyshire. Its Chair Stone has a ledge cut out of its face, like a seat.

row.description: The Samothrace Temple Complex, known as the Sanctuary of the Great Gods, is one of the principal Pan-Hellenic religious sanctuaries, located on the island of Samothrace within the larger Thrace [1]. Built immediately to the west of the ramparts of the city of Samothrace, it was nonetheless independent, as attested to by the dispatch of city ambassadors during festivals [1]. It was celebrated throughout Ancient Greece for its Mystery religion [1]. The temple complex is mentioned by Plato and Aristophanes [1]. During the Hellenistic period, after the investiture of Phillip II, it formed a Macedonian national sanctuary where the successors to Alexander the Great vied to outdo each other's munificence [1]. It remained an important religious site throughout the Roman period [1]. The cult fades from history towards the end of Late Antiquity [1]. The sanctuary occupies three narrow terraces on the west slopes of mount Hagios Georgios, separated by two steep-banked torrents [1].

row.description: Moel Arthur is an Iron Age hillfort in Flintshire, Wales, at the boundary with Denbighshire, about 5 miles east of Denbigh [1]. It is on a prominent hill, height 455.8 metres, in the Clwydian Range; it overlooks the Vale of Clwyd to the west [1]. The oval fort is about 160 metres north–south and 140 metres east–west, enclosing an area of 1.8 hectares [1]. There are two large banks and ditches to the north, where the hill slope is not steep; above the steep south-west, south and east slopes there is a single bank [1]. At the north-east, at the edge of the steeper slopes, there is a narrow inturned entrance with an oblique approach [1]. The form of entrance, and the simple plan of the fort, suggest that it is an early example [1]. In the north and east of the interior there is a broad terrace, and building platforms have been found [1].
row.card: Moel Arthur, an oval Iron Age hillfort of 1.8 hectares, has two large banks and ditches to the north and a narrow inturned entrance at the north-east. Inside, building platforms were found.

row.description: Caister Roman Site is a Roman Saxon Shore fort, located in Caister-on-Sea, Norfolk [1]. It was constructed around AD 200 for use by units of the Roman army and navy, and was occupied until around 370-390 AD [1]. The fort was originally 3.5 ha in size and roughly square in shape, with large stone perimeter walls 4 to 5 m high, earth ramparts and ditches of 175 m in length on all four sides [1]. At the time of its construction, the site of the fort would have been on the north side of an estuary, with a pebbled street from the fort's south gate leading a short distance to a harbour or docks [1]. Between 1951 and 1955, a section of the fort was excavated with the main structures left exposed, including part of the south gate, the western section of the south wall perimeter defences, building foundations, and main road [1]. Finds during the archaeological excavation include four Roman coins of the mid 4th century, as well as seven small hoards, the remains of wattle and daub walling, pottery, glass, part of a pewter plate, and grain [1].
row.card: Caister Roman Site, a Saxon Shore fort constructed around AD 200 for units of the Roman army and navy: a pebbled street would have led from its south gate to a harbour or docks.

row.description: The Shipton Hill Settlement is an archaeological site, a defended settlement of the Iron Age, near Shipton Gorge in Dorset [1]. The site is regarded as a defended settlement, a rare monument type; such sites are found in upland areas of south-west England, sometimes situated in prominent locations but smaller than hillforts [1]. They were occupied by small communities, perhaps a single family group [1]. The oval enclosure has natural slopes to the west and east, but is steepened to the north and south [1]. Near the centre of the enclosure is a small circular mound, diameter 10 metres and height 0.2 metres, on which is a modern trig point; the mound may possibly be a bowl barrow [1]. There has been partial excavation: objects found include Iron Age pottery sherds, hammer stones, flint flakes, scrapers and fragments of quern-stone [1].
row.card: Shipton Hill Settlement is a rare Iron Age defended settlement in Dorset, a type occupied by small communities, perhaps a single family group. Partial excavation found hammer stones.

row.description: Carrigagulla (Irish: Carraig an Ghiolla) is a megalithic complex 2.9 km north-east of Ballinagree, County Cork, Ireland [1]. Carrigagulla A is an 8-metre-diameter (26 ft) stone circle consisting of 16 standing stones circling a central slab [1]. The Carrigagulla NE stone row consists of five stones, four of which have been moved and are now used as gates [1]. The stone row at Carrigagulla SW is built from three stones, one of which has fallen [1].
row.card: Near Ballinagree in County Cork, Carrigagulla gathers a circle of 16 standing stones around a central slab, and a stone row where four of five stones have been moved and now serve as gates.

row.description: The region around Niederstotzingen has been inhabited since pre-historic times [1]. A Celtic Viereckschanze or "four-sided earthworks" has been discovered near modern Niederstotzingen [1]. From the Roman era, a villa rustica has been discovered between Niederstotzingen and Sontheim [1]. During construction in the south part of town, in 1962, a small cemetery from the later half of the 7th century was discovered [1]. The Alamannian cemetery contained the remains of several nobles as well as their animals and valuables [1].
row.card: Near Niederstotzingen, a Celtic four-sided earthwork and a Roman villa rustica were found. In 1962, construction uncovered an Alamannian cemetery of nobles with their animals and valuables.

row.description: Kit's Coty House or Kit's Coty is a chambered long barrow near the village of Aylesford in the southeastern English county of Kent [1]. Constructed circa 4000 BCE, during the Early Neolithic period of British prehistory, today it survives in a ruined state [1]. Archaeologists have established that the monument was built by pastoralist communities shortly after the introduction of agriculture to Britain from continental Europe [1]. Although representing part of an architectural tradition of long barrow building that was widespread across Neolithic Europe, Kit's Coty House belongs to a localised regional variant of barrows produced in the vicinity of the River Medway, now known as the Medway Megaliths [1]. Of these, it lies near to both Little Kit's Coty House and the Coffin Stone on the eastern side of the river [1]. The surviving part of the monument represents three stones covered by a capstone [1]. The mound and flanking ditches have largely been ploughed flat but remain visible from aerial photographs [1].
row.card: Near Aylesford in Kent, three stones still carry the capstone of Kit's Coty House, a long barrow built circa 4000 BCE, its mound largely ploughed flat yet visible from aerial photographs.

row.description: Easter Island is an island and special territory of Chile in the southeastern Pacific Ocean, at the southeasternmost point of the Polynesian Triangle in Oceania [1]. The first recorded European contact with the island was on April 5, 1722, Easter Sunday [1]. Easter Island is a volcanic island, consisting mainly of three extinct coalesced volcanoes: Terevaka forms the bulk of the island, while two other volcanoes, Poike and Rano Kau, form the eastern and southern headlands and give the island its roughly triangular shape [1]. Almost all moai were carved from compressed, easily worked solidified volcanic ash or tuff, found at a single site on the side of the extinct volcano Rano Raraku [1]. The native islanders who carved them used only stone hand chisels, mainly basalt toki, which lie in place all over the quarry [1]. Of the 313 known ahu, 125 carried moai – usually just one, probably because of the shortness of the moai period and transportation difficulties [1]. Ahu Tongariki, one km from Rano Raraku, had the most and tallest moai, 15 in total [1].
row.card: On Easter Island, the native carvers of the moai used only stone hand chisels, mainly basalt toki, which lie in place all over the quarry. Of 313 known ahu, 125 carried moai, usually one.

row.description: The Caves of Poço Velho are located in the centre of Cascais in the Lisbon district of Portugal [1]. The caves were first explored in 1879 by the geologist, Carlos Ribeiro [1]. However, subsequent work has found that the main occupation of the caves took place in the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods (4th and 3rd millennia BC) [1]. Evidence points to their use as a necropolis, with around 115 burials having been identified [1]. In 1942, Afonso do Paço carried out the second major exploration of the caves and between 1945 and 1947, the archaeologist, Abreu Nunes, carried out new excavations that discovered different funerary remains, including: polished and chipped stone artefacts; limestone votive offerings, such as cylindrical idols; decorated schist slabs, and ceramics [1].
row.card: In Cascais, evidence points to use of the Caves of Poço Velho as a necropolis, with around 115 burials identified. Finds include limestone votive offerings and decorated schist slabs.

row.description: Praetorium Agrippinae was a Roman settlement in the province of Lower Germania, in the area of the Cananefates, located in modern-day Valkenburg [1]. It was an army encampment on the Old Rhine, on the northern border of the Roman Empire, the limes [1]. Praetorium Agrippinae is mentioned on the Tabula Peutingeriana between the castella of Matilo in the east and Lugdunum Batavorum to the west [1]. The fort was built in the current centre of Valkenburg, and was at first fortified by a palisaded earthen wall and three moats [1]. To the southeast of the fortress, a large civil settlement developed, stretching for approx. 1 km along the via militaris [1]. It was inhabited between approx. 70 and 240 AD [1]. Archaeological investigations have uncovered living quarters, storehouses and granaries, and possibly a bath house [1]. Investigations started in 1875, but the main excavations were done between 1941 and 1953 under the direction of Albert Egges van Giffen [1].
row.card: On the Old Rhine, on the northern border of the Roman Empire, Praetorium Agrippinae was an army camp at first fortified by a palisaded earthen wall and three moats. Digs found storehouses.

row.description: Fishbourne Roman Palace or Fishbourne Villa is in the village of Fishbourne, near Chichester in West Sussex [1]. Extensive alterations were made in the second and third centuries AD, when many of the original black and white mosaics were overlaid with more sophisticated coloured work [1]. The site was accidentally discovered in 1805 [1]. Workers discovered 13-foot-wide pavement as well as fragments of columns [1]. The first buildings on the site were granaries, over 33 m long, apparently a supply base for the Roman army constructed in the early part of the conquest in 43 AD [1]. Later, two residential timber-frame buildings were constructed, one with clay and mortar floors and plaster walls which appears to have been a house of some comfort [1]. These buildings were demolished around 60 AD and replaced nearby with an elaborate and substantial stone-walled villa, or proto-palace, in about 65 AD which included a courtyard garden with colonnades and a bath suite, together with two other buildings [1]. It was decorated with wall paintings, stucco mouldings and opus sectile marble polychrome panels [1].
row.card: Near Chichester, Fishbourne Roman Palace was built around 75–80 AD, four wings around a formal courtyard garden. Many of its black and white mosaics were later overlaid with coloured work.

row.description: Knossos lies on Kephala hill, in the valley of the Kairatos river, within the modern municipality of Heraklion, about 5 km south of the historic centre [1]. The earliest known settlement at Knossos dates to about 7000 BC, during the early Neolithic period [1]. The first palace at Knossos was constructed around 1900 BC [1]. The Second Palace period, from about 1700 to 1450 BC, was the height of Minoan Knossos [1]. After about 1450 BC, Knossos became an important Mycenaean administrative centre [1]. In the Archaic and Classical periods, Knossos was a major Cretan city-state [1]. In 1900, Arthur Evans began large-scale excavations at Knossos [1]. The Palace of Minos is the dominant archaeological feature at Knossos [1].
row.card: Knossos lies on Kephala hill; its earliest known settlement dates to about 7000 BC and its first palace was built around 1900 BC. The Palace of Minos is the dominant archaeological feature.

row.description: Human settlement in the territory of present-day Petrovaradin has been traced as far back as the Stone Age (about 4500 BC) [1]. This region was conquered by Celts (in the 4th century BC) and Romans (in the 1st century BC) [1]. The Celts founded the first fortress at this location [1]. It was part of the tribal state of the Scordisci, which had its capital in Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) [1]. During the Roman administration, a larger fortress was built with the name Cusum and was included into Roman Pannonia [1]. Subsequently, the fortress was included into the Pannonia Inferior and the Pannonia Secunda [1].
row.card: Petrovaradin's region fell to Celts in the 4th century BC and to Romans in the 1st century BC. Under Roman administration a fortress named Cusum rose here, part of Roman Pannonia.

row.description: Grime's Graves is a large Neolithic flint mining complex in Norfolk, England [1]. It lies 8 km north east from Brandon, Suffolk in the East of England [1]. It was worked between c. 2600 and c. 2300 BC, although production may have continued through the Bronze and Iron Ages and later [1]. The scheduled monument extends over an area of some 37 ha and consists of at least 433 shafts dug into the natural chalk to reach seams of flint [1]. The largest shafts are more than 14 m deep and 12 m in diameter at the surface [1]. An upper 'topstone' and middle 'wallstone' seam of flint was dug through on the way to the deeper third 'floorstone' seam which most interested the miners [1]. The miners used picks fashioned from the antler of red deer [1]. Grime's Graves was first extensively explored by the archaeologist William Greenwell in 1868 [1].
row.card: In the chalk of Norfolk, the Neolithic miners of Grime's Graves sank at least 433 shafts, digging with red deer antler picks through topstone and wallstone toward the floorstone flint.

row.description: The pyramid of Khentkaus I or step tomb of Khentkaus I is a Fourth Dynasty two-stepped tomb built for the Queen Mother Khentkaus I in Giza [1]. A nearly square block of bedrock, around which the stone had been quarried for the Giza pyramids, was utilised to construct her tomb and encased with fine white Tura limestone [1]. South-west of the tomb was a long boat pit [1]. A chapel was built into the tomb superstructure, with a large granite entrance bearing the queen's name and titles [1]. A settlement was built around Khentkaus' tomb, and probably occupied by priests of her mortuary cult until the end of the Sixth Dynasty [1]. Along a causeway leading from the chapel through the town, ten carefully planned homes were built, suggesting that the town was designed and not the result of natural urban development [1]. The town was further outfitted with granaries and a large water tank [1].
row.card: At Giza, the Tomb of Queen Khentkawes I was encased in fine white Tura limestone, and a chapel built into its superstructure had a large granite entrance bearing the queen's name and titles.

row.description: San Pawl Milqi are the ruins of a Roman period agricultural villa and pagan temple [1]. The site has been in use since prehistoric times; a couple of tombs date back to the Zebbug and possibly the Borg in-Nadur phases of the Maltese Bronze Age [1]. The first building on the site was probably built in the Phoenician-Punic period, when the site was used intermittently for agriculture [1]. A small number of structures remain from this period and one burial bears a neo-Punic inscription [1]. In the Roman period, the site’s position on the slopes of a fertile valley and vicinity to the Roman harbour at Salina meant that it was ideally suited to the production of olive oil [1]. The establishment was expanded; the original central courtyard was transformed into an industrial area [1]. Although the remains of the villa have long been well known, scientific excavations, led by the Missione Archeologica Italiana a Malta, did not commence until 1963 [1].
row.card: San Pawl Milqi, ruins of a Roman period villa and pagan temple, lay near the Roman harbour at Salina, ideally suited to olive oil. One burial there bears a neo-Punic inscription.

row.description: The Luxor Temple is a large Ancient Egyptian temple complex located on the east bank of the Nile River in the city of Luxor and was constructed around 1400 BC [1]. In Egyptian it was known as ipet resyt, "the southern sanctuary" [1]. It was one of the two primary temples on the east bank, the other being Karnak [1]. To the rear of the temple are chapels built by Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty, and Alexander [1]. Other parts of the temple were built by Tutankhamun and Ramesses II [1]. During the Roman era, the temple and its surroundings were a legionary fortress and the home of the Roman government in the area [1]. The Luxor Temple was built with sandstone from the Gebel el-Silsila area [1]. At the Luxor Temple, the two obelisks flanking the entrance were not the same height, but they created the illusion that they were [1].
row.card: On the Nile's east bank, Luxor Temple was built around 1400 BC of sandstone from the Gebel el-Silsila area, with parts by Tutankhamun. In the Roman era it was a legionary fortress.

row.description: Chevdar is a Neolithic archeological site near Kazanluk in Bulgaria [1]. An early Neolithic house was found that would have had wooden walls, marked by post holes [1]. It was plastered with clay with the remains of a hearth also found [1]. Carbonised seeds of emmer, barley and bitter vetch were found [1]. These results were found using one of the earliest uses of flotation technology in archaeobotany [1].
row.card: At Chevdar, post holes mark an early Neolithic house that would have had wooden walls, plastered with clay. A hearth's remains and carbonised emmer, barley and bitter vetch seeds were found.

row.description: The Six Hills are a collection of Roman barrows situated alongside the old Great North Road on Six Hills Common in Stevenage, Hertfordshire [1]. They are classed as a Scheduled Ancient Monument and are protected by law [1]. They form the largest surviving Roman barrow group in England [1]. For almost two thousand years, travellers along the Roman road that eventually became the Great North Road have passed these six large mounds [1].
row.card: For almost two thousand years, travellers along the Roman road that eventually became the Great North Road have passed Six Hills, a collection of Roman barrows in Stevenage, Hertfordshire.

row.description: The Castro of Cidadelhe is a Portuguese castro in civil parish of Cidadelhe, in the municipality of Mesão Frio [1]. Cidadelhe was a fortified settlement of a proto-historic nature, later occupied by Roman and Medieval residents [1]. The castro is located in an isolated rural environment on a hilltop [1]. Two lines of walls encircle the castle and roadways/paths, composed of schist rock [1]. In the interior of the ruins are several remains of residences, of a circular design, excavated by recent archaeologists [1].
row.card: The Castro of Cidadelhe crowns an isolated rural hilltop in Mesão Frio: a fortified settlement of a proto-historic nature, later occupied by Roman and Medieval residents.

row.description: Following a sinuous path, at 85 km the aqueduct of the Gier is the longest known of the Roman aqueducts [1]. Leaving the uplands of the Massif du Pilat, department of the Loire, the aqueduct hugs the surface relief and crosses the department of the Rhone, passing through Mornant, Orliénas, Chaponost and Sainte-Foy-lès-Lyon to terminate at Lyon [1]. In its extent, it draws upon the whole repertory of Roman techniques of aqueduct building, taking a slope that averages 0.1% [1]. There are 73 km of covered ditches laid with a concrete culvert 3 m high and 1.5 m wide [1]. The aqueduct passes through 11 tunnels, one of which, near Mornant, is 825 m in extent [1]. Four inverted siphon tunnels cross the particularly deep and wide river valleys of the Durèze, the Garon, the Yzeron and the Trion on pipe bridges raised on high arches [1]. The Gier aqueduct was built in a single great campaign, since no part of it could have served until it was completed; it must have taken years [1].
row.card: Winding 85 km from the Massif du Pilat to Lyon, the Aqueduct of the Gier passes through 11 tunnels and crosses deep river valleys on pipe bridges raised on high arches.

row.description: Rather than depicting only the familiar herbivores that predominate in Paleolithic cave art, i.e. horses, aurochs, mammoths, etc., the walls of the Chauvet Cave feature many predatory animals, e.g., cave lions, leopards, bears, and cave hyenas [1]. There are also paintings of rhinoceroses [1]. Typical of most cave art, there are no paintings of complete human figures, although there are two partial "Venus" figures: one within a niche or vestibule of the End Chamber, and the other on a roughly conical or dental-shaped pendant several metres away; both are composed of what appears to be a vulva attached to an incomplete pair of legs [1]. Above the pendant Venus, and in contact with it, is a bison head, which has led some to describe the composite drawing as a Minotaur [1]. There are a few panels of red ochre hand prints and hand stencils made by blowing pigment over hands pressed against the cave surface [1].
row.card: Rhinoceroses are painted on the walls of Chauvet Cave, where red ochre hands were stenciled by blowing pigment over them. Above a Venus figure, a bison head made some see a Minotaur.

row.description: The Ali Murad Mound is an archaeological site situated at Johi Tehsil, in Dadu District of Sindh, Pakistan [1]. The site was explored as well as named by archaeologist N. G. Majumdar [1]. It is located 20 miles from Dadu towards the southwest [1]. It is eight miles from Ghazi Shah Mound and 14 miles to the south of Johi town [1]. At the top of the mound, an ancient hamlet was discovered surrounded by defensive walls built with stone blocks [1].
row.card: Ali Murad Mound lies 20 miles southwest of Dadu. At its top, an ancient hamlet was found ringed by defensive walls of stone blocks, and N. G. Majumdar explored and named the site.

row.description: Blakey Topping standing stones is a small group of standing stones near the Hole of Horcum in the North York Moors [1]. It sits at the foot of Blakey Topping hill [1]. There are at least four standing stones currently surviving in this group, although some of them are of uncertain status [1]. The tallest stone is 1.9 metres high and is much-weathered and leaning [1]. A second stone is 1.0 metres high and appears to have had its top broken off [1]. A third stone is 1.3 metres high but has been roughly squared off and is currently being used as a gate post [1]. A fourth stone, 1.4 metres high, is found in an old field bank and is much-weathered and leaning [1].
row.card: Near the Hole of Horcum, at least four of the Blakey Topping Standing Stones survive, some of uncertain status. The tallest is 1.9 metres, much-weathered and leaning.

row.description: The Temple of Ptah is a shrine located within the large Precinct of Amun-Re at Karnak, in Luxor, Egypt [1]. It lies to the north of the main Amun temple, just within the boundary wall [1]. The temple consists of six small gateways built close together [1]. The sixth gateway crosses through the pylons and runs through directly into the central sanctuary, where the statue of Ptah stands [1]. Excavations have found figurines of baboons and the gods Osiris, Mut, and Bastet, as well as stelae marked with the name of Ptah [1].
row.card: At Karnak, the Temple of Ptah has six small gateways built close together; the sixth runs directly into the central sanctuary, where the statue of Ptah stands. Baboon figurines were found.

row.description: The Tahai Ceremonial Complex is an archaeological site on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in Chilean Polynesia [1]. Restored in 1974 by American archaeologist William Mulloy, Tahai comprises three principal ahu from north to south: Ko Te Riku (with restored eyes), Tahai, and Vai Ure [1]. Like other Mulloy restoration projects at Ahu Akivi, the ceremonial village of Orongo and Vinapu, the ceremonial center at Tahai now constitutes an integral part of the Rapa Nui National Park [1]. William Mulloy and his wife Emily Ross Mulloy are buried at Tahai [1].
row.card: On Rapa Nui, three principal ahu run north to south at the Tahai Ceremonial Complex, Ko Te Riku with its restored eyes. Archaeologist William Mulloy and his wife are buried here.

row.description: Trevelgue Head, also known as Porth Island, is a headland north-east of Newquay, Cornwall, England [1]. It is the site of an Iron Age promontory fort with defensive ramparts and two round barrows dating from the early Bronze Age [1]. The peninsula is connected to the mainland at the eastern end; on the south is a natural harbour [1]. On the east side there are defensive earthworks [1]. There is a single bank and ditch on the wider part of the peninsula near the mainland [1]. The wide enclosure between this and the ramparts further west is protected by sea-cliffs on the northern side; on the south side there is a smaller drop to the sea [1]. There is a gap in the peninsula, crossed by a modern bridge where there may have been originally a land-bridge; immediately before this there are three massive banks and ditches [1]. About 600 items of worked stone, over 4,000 shards of pottery, and objects of tin, copper and iron and glass were found [1].
row.card: On Trevelgue Head, three massive banks and ditches lie just before a gap crossed by a modern bridge. Over 4,000 shards of pottery and objects of tin, copper, iron and glass were found.

row.description: Xochitecatl [ʃot͡ʃiˈtekat͡ɬ] is a pre-Columbian archaeological site located in the Mexican State of Tlaxcala, 18 km southwest of Tlaxcala city [1]. The major architecture dates to the Middle Preclassic Period (1000–400 BC) but occupation continued, with one major interruption, until the Late Classic, when the site was abandoned [1]. The ruins cover an area of 12 hectares on top of a volcanic dome [1]. By the period spanning 350 BC to 100 AD, Xochitecatl had become the centre of a powerful chiefdom exercising control over a large portion of western Tlaxcala [1]. Between 600 AD and 950 AD Xochitecatl was reoccupied when parts of the site were reused as a secondary ceremonial centre within the extended urban area of Cacaxtla [1]. Major excavations were undertaken at the site in 1993-4 by Mari Carmen Serra Puche with the goal of exploring the principal structures around the site core [1].
row.card: On a volcanic dome in Tlaxcala, the ruins of Xochitecatl cover 12 hectares. Once the centre of a powerful chiefdom, parts of it were reused as a secondary ceremonial centre of Cacaxtla.

row.description: Pantikapaion was an ancient Greek city on the eastern shore of Crimea, which the Greeks called Taurica [1]. The city lay on the western side of the Cimmerian Bosporus, and was founded by Milesians in the late 7th or early 6th century BC, on a hill later named Mount Mithridat [1]. Its ruins now lie in the modern city of Kerch [1]. The city minted silver coins from the 5th century BC and gold and bronze coins from the 4th century BC [1]. At its greatest extent it occupied 100 hectares [1]. In the 5th–4th centuries BC, the city became the residence first of the Archaeanactids and then of the Spartocids, dynasties of Thracian kings of Bosporus, and was hence itself sometimes called Bosporus [1]. Its economic decline in the 4th–3rd centuries BC was the result of the Sarmatian conquest of the steppes and the growing competition of Egyptian grain [1]. Mithridates took his life in Pantikapaion, when, after his defeat in a war against Rome, his son and heir Pharnaces and citizens of Pantikapaion turned against him [1].
row.card: Milesians founded Pantikapaion, a Greek city that minted silver, gold and bronze coins, on a hill later named Mount Mithridat. Here Mithridates took his life as his son turned against him.

row.description: Stravomyti Cave is an ancient Minoan cave on Crete [1]. Stravomyti Cave is 400 meters above sea level on Mt. Juktas' southwest slope [1]. Stravomyti Cave first saw use during Neolithic times, as a refuge and burial [1]. During the Early Minoan period, the quality of pottery suggests that people lived in the caves [1]. Thereafter, it was used for storage and worship [1]. The cave may have once been a shrine to a female deity - Artemis, Diktynna or perhaps Eileithyia [1].
row.card: On the southwest slope of Mount Juktas, Stravomyti Cave first saw use in Neolithic times as a refuge and burial, and may once have been a shrine to Artemis, Diktynna or perhaps Eileithyia.

row.description: Piruro (possibly from Quechua for whorl) is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is situated in the Huánuco Region, Huamalíes Province, Tantamayo District [1]. The complex consists of two parts named Piruro I and Piruro II [1]. This archaeological zone has had a long occupation: Its first vestiges date from 3000 to 2500 years B.C. (Final Preceramic), and they extend until the Inca Empire (Late Horizon) [1]. The Fortress of Piruro II can be found on the right side of the river Tantamayo over 3.8 km above sea level [1]. The fortress is composed of walls built with stones hewn in squared shape and uniform size [1]. The building is a five-story structure with rectangular doors and windows on its front area [1]. Currently the building is enclosed by stone walls measuring approximately 1 1/2 meters in height [1].
row.card: On the right side of the river Tantamayo, over 3.8 km above sea level, Piruro keeps a five-story building, its walls built with stones hewn in squared shape and uniform size.

row.description: Toro Muerto is a collection of ancient petroglyphs in the Peruvian coastal desert, found in the Castilla province in the region Arequipa in Peru [1]. The site contains some 3000 volcanic rocks with petroglyphs dating back to the Wari culture, active from 500 to 1000 AD [1].
row.card: In the Peruvian coastal desert of the Arequipa region, Toro Muerto holds some 3000 volcanic rocks bearing ancient petroglyphs, a gallery of images beneath the desert sky.

row.description: Tiryns is a Mycenaean archaeological site in Argolis in the Peloponnese [1]. Tiryns was a hill fort with occupation ranging back seven thousand years, from before the beginning of the Bronze Age [1]. It reached its height of importance between 1400 and 1200 BC, when it became one of the most important centers of the Mycenaean world, and in particular in Argolis [1]. Its most notable features were its palace, its Cyclopean tunnels and especially its walls, which gave the city its Homeric epithet of "mighty walled Tiryns" [1]. In c. 1300 BC, the citadel and lower town had a population of 10,000 people covering 20–25 hectares [1]. Despite the destruction of the palace in c. 1200 BC, the city population continued to increase and by 1150 BC it had a population of 15,000 people [1]. In the post-palatial LH IIIC period (c. 1180 BC), an extensive deposit of precious items, including gold and silver objects and a fifteenth-century BC Minoan signet ring, was made in a cauldron in Tiryns's lower town [1].
row.card: Its walls won it the Homeric epithet mighty walled Tiryns. Its features included a palace and Cyclopean tunnels, and in the lower town a cauldron held gold, silver and a Minoan signet ring.

row.description: The villa of Lucullus was an extensive and sumptuous ancient Roman villa built in the first century BC in Naples by the famous gourmet, general and consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus [1]. The villa was equipped with piers that stretched out into the sea, a very rich library, fish ponds and moray eel farms and lavish gardens with peach trees imported from Persia which for the time were a novelty along with the cherry trees he brought in from Cerasus [1]. At some point after the death of Lucullus (57/56 BC), the villa passed to the Roman emperor; later, under Valentinian III (419-455), it was transformed into a fortress, and since then has been called the castellum Lucullanum, and was the place of exile of Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman Emperor [1]. Remains of the villa, given its enormous area, are visible at several places in the city of Naples [1]. The largest and perhaps most important nucleus is located in the cellar of the Castel dell'Ovo situated on the islet of Megaride, the so-called "hall of columns" derived from the Roman columns still standing [1].
row.card: Built in Naples in the first century BC, the Villa of Lucullus had piers stretching into the sea. Its remains are visible at several places, and Roman columns still stand in a castle cellar.

row.description: La Grotte des Fées is a cave located in Châtelperron, in the central French department of Allier [1]. The name refers to three caves, of which one is collapsed [1]. The caves are located in the commune of Châtelperron, about 1 km north of the town [1]. Two interlinked caves were first discovered around 1840, perhaps in 1848, during the construction of the railway which used to link the mines from Bert to Dompierre-sur-Besbre [1]. A third cave (today collapsed), was discovered in 1867 by Bailleau [1]. Several thousand flint blades and mammoth tusks of over 2 metres (6 ft 7 in) long were found [1]. The last research, from 1951 to 1954 and in 1962, was led by Henri Delporte and revealed back blades of flint, burins, drills and scrapers [1].
row.card: La Grotte des Fées: two interlinked caves discovered around 1840, perhaps in 1848, during railway construction. Several thousand flint blades and mammoth tusks over 2 metres long were found.

row.description: King's Castle is an Iron Age enclosed hilltop settlement at the south-western edge of the Mendip Hills near Wells in Somerset [1]. Though there are many prehistoric sites in the surrounding area, it remains one of the earliest known settlements in the immediate vicinity of Wells, and may have been a precursor to the present day city [1]. It consists of two or three interlinked sub-enclosures, with what appears to be a field system extending to the east; an unusual layout, the site remains relatively little studied and has not been archaeologically excavated [1]. It is a Scheduled Ancient Monument, and shares its name with the surrounding King's Castle Wood—today a Somerset Wildlife Trust nature reserve—though this name is probably a modern invention [1].
row.card: A Scheduled Ancient Monument, King's Castle is a hilltop settlement near Wells in Somerset, its interlinked enclosures never archaeologically excavated. Was it the city's precursor?

row.description: The Roman Theatre (Italian: Teatro romano di Benevento) is an ancient Roman edifice in Benevento [1]. It was built in the 2nd century by emperor Hadrian near the city's cardo maximus (126 AD) [1]. Abandoned in Lombard times, it is now surrounded by the medieval Rione (district) Triggio [1]. The theatre has a semicircular plan with a diameter of 90 meters: it could originally house some 10,000/15,000 spectators [1]. The cavea has mostly survived [1]. The large scene features remains of three monumental gates which led to the orchestra; at the latter's side are the remains of the parodoi, of which the right one has kept the pavement mosaic and the polychrome marble walls, which likely characterized most of the theatre originally [1].
row.card: In Benevento, the Roman Theatre that Hadrian built in 126 AD was abandoned in Lombard times and is now surrounded by the medieval Triggio district. One passage keeps its mosaic pavement.

row.description: Newgrange is a prehistoric monument in County Meath in Ireland, placed on a rise overlooking the River Boyne [1]. Newgrange is the main monument in the Brú na Bóinne complex, a World Heritage Site that also includes the passage tombs of Knowth and Dowth, as well as other henges, burial mounds and standing stones [1]. Newgrange consists of a large circular mound with an inner stone passageway and cruciform chamber [1]. Burnt and unburnt human bones and possible grave goods or votive offerings were found in this chamber [1]. The monument has a striking façade made mostly of white quartz cobblestones and ringed by engraved kerbstones [1]. Many of the larger stones of Newgrange are covered in megalithic art [1]. The mound is 85 metres wide at its widest point and 12 metres high, and covers 4,500 square metres of ground [1]. Excavations in the late 1960s and early 1970s revealed seven "marbles", four pendants, two beads, a used flint flake, a bone chisel, and fragments of bone pins and points [1].
row.card: Above the River Boyne, Newgrange shows a façade made mostly of white quartz, ringed by engraved kerbstones. Its stone passage leads to a cruciform chamber where burnt bones were found.

row.description: Sammallahdenmäki is a Bronze Age burial site in Finland in Rauma, in the region of Satakunta [1]. The burial site is located on a long ridge in a remote area off the road to Tampere from Rauma [1]. The 33 burial cairns making up the site are arranged into distinct clusters along the crest of the ridge [1]. Each cairn was constructed from granite boulders quarried from the cliff face below the ridge or collected on site, in typical Bronze Age fashion [1]. Two unusual cairns are the Huilun pitkä raunio ("long ruin of Huilu"), which is surrounded by an ancient stone wall, and the Kirkonlaattia ("Church Floor"), an unusual rectangular cairn covering 16 x 19 metres with a flat top [1]. Four of the cairns were excavated by archaeologist Volter Högman in 1891, including Huilun pitkä raunio and Kirkonlaattia [1].
row.card: At Sammallahdenmäki in Rauma, the Kirkonlaattia, or Church Floor, is a rectangular cairn of granite boulders covering 16 x 19 metres, with a flat top. Volter Högman excavated it in 1891.

A site of archaeological and historical interest, it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural site on 27 June 2002 [1].

row.description: Ta' Kaċċatura is an archaeological complex on the outskirts of Birżebbuġa, in southern Malta [1]. The complex includes a rustic Roman villa and a number of underground cisterns [1]. The villa confirms the presence of a thriving olive oil industry in this part of the Maltese islands [1]. The remains rest on a long, flat ridge flanked by two valleys, Wied Dalam to the north-east and Wied Żembaq to the south-west [1]. The site was mostly untouched in the late 19th century, with investigations only resuming under the direction of Thomas Ashby and Temi Żammit in 1915 [1]. Ashby's descriptions remain the principal sources of information on the rustic villa [1].
row.card: A long, flat ridge flanked by Wied Dalam and Wied Żembaq carries Ta' Kaċċatura: underground cisterns and a rustic Roman villa that confirms a thriving olive oil industry.

row.description: The baths of an ancient Roman villa were discovered at Masseria De Carolis in Pollena Trocchia in 1988 and subsequently exposed [1]. The baths were built after the 79 AD eruption and before the mid-2nd century [1]. The eruptions of Vesuvius of 472 buried the lower floors but clearance work was done and occupation then continued in the upper levels until it was completely buried in the 505 and 512 eruptions [1]. The site was first discovered during construction of apartment blocks but the builders tried to destroy it as a hindrance to their work [1]. The Apolline Project identified the site and from 2005 it was cleared and annual excavations started [1]. 10 rooms of baths with massive structures have been discovered on two floors [1].
row.card: At Pollena Trocchia, Vesuvius buried the lower floors of a Roman villa's baths in 472, yet occupation went on in the upper levels until a further eruption, either that of 505 or 512.

row.description: The Dimini area contains both a Mycenean settlement and a Neolithic settlement [1]. The Neolithic settlement in Dimini was discovered near the end of the 19th century and was first excavated by the archaeologists Christos Tsountas and Valerios Stais [1]. Dimini culture is well known for its abstract painted vessels [1]. Dimini ware is characteristic of the Later Neolithic period in eastern Thessaly, although it was traded and imitated outside the region and has been identified as far away as Cakran in Albania [1]. In 1977, George Chourmouziadis continued excavations at the Neolithic settlement [1]. Excavations of the Mycenean settlement in Dimini began in 1980 by V. Adrimi-Sismani [1].
row.card: The Dimini area holds a Neolithic settlement and a Mycenean one. Dimini culture is well known for abstract painted vessels; Dimini ware has been identified as far away as Cakran in Albania.

row.description: The Salina Catacombs are a cluster of small catacombs located near the Church of the Annunciation in Salina, Naxxar [1]. Although small when compared to the catacombs of St. Paul and St. Agatha in Rabat, they are an important record of the sizeable community that must have lived in the area in around the last half of the first millennium AD [1]. The catacombs open on to a low ridge facing a now lost Roman harbour [1]. The site comprises five hypogea cut into the vertical surface of a small quarry [1]. The most impressive hypogeum is adorned with two decorated pillars, an agape table and two baldacchino tombs [1]. The window tombs that surround the agape table suggest that it was an important feature of the catacomb [1]. At least two of the window tombs are lavishly decorated with reliefs depicting palm fronds and other spiraled patterns [1]. The palm fronds, together with a number of incised crosses, are proof of the Christian origins of the burial site [1].
row.card: The Salina Catacombs open on to a low ridge facing a now lost Roman harbour. Their most impressive hypogeum is adorned with two decorated pillars, an agape table and two baldacchino tombs.

row.description: The Schalkholz Passage Grave, also known as Schalkholz-Vierth is a megalithic burial site of the Neolithic period and of the Funnelbeaker culture in Vierth, a district of Schalkholz in the province of Schleswig-Holstein in Germany [1]. During the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age, it was used for a secondary burial site and was expanded upon [1]. It has the Sprockhoff number 139 and the site number LA 33 or Heide LA 5 [1]. The grave was archaeologically investigated in 1969 and 1970 and was afterwards moved to the nearby town of Heide [1]. In 2021 it was moved back to Schalkholz [1].
row.card: A Neolithic burial of the Funnelbeaker culture, the Schalkholz Passage Grave was archaeologically investigated in 1969 and 1970, then moved to Heide. In 2021 it went back to Schalkholz.

row.description: Altun Ha is the name given to the ruins of an ancient Maya city in Belize, located in the Belize District about 50 kilometres north of Belize City and about 10 kilometres west of the shore of the Caribbean Sea [1]. The site covers an area of about 8 square kilometres [1]. The largest of Altun Ha's temple-pyramids, the "Temple of the Masonry Altars", is 16 metres high [1]. Starting in 1964, an archaeological team led by Dr. David Pendergast of the Royal Ontario Museum began extensive excavations and restorations of the site, which continued through 1970 [1]. Most of the information on Altun Ha comes from the Classic Period from about A.D. 400 to A.D. 900, when the city was at its largest [1]. The earliest structures found at Altun Ha, found in Zone C, are two round platforms that date to about BC 900−800 [1]. Over 800 pieces of jade have been recovered at the site [1]. By the beginning of the eleventh century, the site of Altun Ha was completely abandoned [1].
row.card: Over 800 pieces of jade have been recovered at Altun Ha, where the Temple of the Masonry Altars is 16 metres high. By the beginning of the eleventh century, the site was abandoned.

row.description: Björkö is an island in Lake Mälaren in eastern-central Sweden [1]. The oldest of the ancient remains on the island is a small burial ground on the elevated section on the southern part of the island [1]. The shrine comprises nine stone structures, of which two are burnt mounds and one is a cairn known as Ingas grav [1]. Their character and elevated location indicate they belonged to a temporary Bronze Age settlement (1800-500 BC), by people who visited the island for seasonal hunting and fishing [1]. The first permanent settlement on the island dates back to the late Germanic Iron Age (400-800 AD) [1].
row.card: On Björkö, the oldest remains are a burial ground on the elevated south. A shrine of nine stone structures, one a cairn called Ingas grav, points to Bronze Age seasonal hunters and fishers.

row.description: As an ancient city, lying off the east coast, Mytilene was initially confined to a small island just offshore that later was joined to Lesbos, creating a north and south harbor [1]. The early harbors of Mytilene were linked during ancient times by a channel 700 m long and 30 m wide [1]. The Roman writer Longus speaks of white stone bridges linking the two sides [1]. Salvage excavations carried out by the Archaeological Service in many areas of the city have revealed sites going back to the Early Bronze Age although most have been much later (Hellenistic and Roman) [1]. Particularly significant is a large stoa over a hundred metres long recently dug on the North Harbour of the city [1]. It is clear from various remains in different parts of the city that Mytilene was indeed laid out on a grid plan as the Roman architect Vitruvius had written [1].
row.card: In ancient Mytilene, a channel 700 m long and 30 m wide linked the early harbors, and the Roman writer Longus speaks of white stone bridges linking the two sides.

row.description: The White Horse Stone is a name given to two separate sarsen megaliths on the slopes of Blue Bell Hill, near the village of Aylesford in the south-eastern English county of Kent [1]. The Lower White Horse Stone was destroyed prior to 1834, at which time the surviving Upper White Horse Stone took on its name and folkloric associations [1]. Various archaeologists have suggested—although not proven—that the stones were each part of chambered long barrows constructed in the fourth millennium BC [1]. Excavation has revealed the existence of an Early Neolithic longhouse near to the stone [1]. The Upper White Horse Stone is 2.9 metres in length, 1.65 metres in height, and about 0.6 metres thick [1]. The White Horse Stone is situated in "a narrow strip of woodland", known as Westfield Wood, which is adjacent to the Pilgrim's Way [1]. To the south of the White Horse Stone was a building—termed "Structure 4806" by its excavators in the 2000s—that was constructed in the Early Neolithic period [1]. Radiocarbon dating from the site suggests a usage date of between 4110-3820 and 3780-3530 calibrated BC [1].
row.card: On the slopes of Blue Bell Hill in Kent, the White Horse Stone took on the name and folklore of a second stone destroyed before 1834. Near it, excavators found an Early Neolithic longhouse.

row.description: Llansteffan Castle (Welsh: Castell Llansteffan) is a privately owned castle in Llansteffan, Carmarthenshire, Wales, overlooking the River Towy estuary in Carmarthen Bay [1]. The castle sits on a much older Iron Age promontory fort, proving Llansteffan has been inhabited for several millennia [1]. The hill where the castle stands commands the River Towy estuary [1]. The original earthworks can still be seen and were used as part of the modern castle's defence system—the castle proper rests within the earthwork rings [1].
row.card: Llansteffan Castle rests within the earthwork rings of a much older Iron Age promontory fort. The original earthworks can still be seen, and were used as part of its defence system.

row.description: Santa Verna is a megalithic site in Xagħra on the island of Gozo, Malta [1]. The site was originally occupied by a village and a megalithic temple [1]. The site takes its name from a chapel dedicated to Saint Venera that once stood close to the temple [1]. Santa Verna was originally a prehistoric village, and the earliest pottery remains date back to around 5000 BC, during the Għar Dalam phase [1]. The temple itself was built in the following centuries and it had a trefoil shape, which was typical of the time [1]. The only remains of the temple that survive today are three upright megaliths, another three horizontal blocks lining their eastern side, and the earth floor which makes it possible to see the temple's original outline [1]. The site was excavated in 1911 by Thomas Ashby and R. N. Bradley [1]. During the excavations, two complete skeletons and several incomplete ones were found, including one of a child [1].
row.card: On Gozo, Santa Verna takes its name from a chapel of Saint Venera that once stood close to the temple. Excavations in 2015 revealed the temple's five-apsed plan of the Ġgantija phase.

row.description: Vinovia or Vinovium was a Roman fort and settlement situated just over 1 mile to the north of the town of Bishop Auckland on the banks of the River Wear in County Durham [1]. The fort was probably established around AD 79 to guard the crossing of the River Wear by Dere Street, the main Roman road between York, Hadrian's Wall and Scotland [1]. Sitting atop a hill 15 metres above the Wear, Binchester was the largest Roman fort in County Durham [1]. Archaeologists found four coins of Vespasian that seem to corroborate that initial building was related to Agricola's march northward into the territory of the Brigantes [1]. The cuneus Frisorum Vinoviensium and the equites catafractariorum have been mentioned in inscriptions from the site [1]. By the early 6th century, a small Anglo-Saxon cemetery had been founded, and the demolition of the fort's buildings for reclamation of the materials had started, some of which were eventually used in the construction of the nearby 7th-century Escomb Church [1].
row.card: Vinovia, a Roman fort on a hill 15 metres above the Wear, was probably built to guard Dere Street's crossing. By the early 6th century its buildings were being demolished for materials.

row.description: Louisenlund, some 3.5 kilometres east of Østermarie on the Danish island of Bornholm, is a site with one of Denmark's largest collection of megaliths [1]. The stones stand alone or in small groups [1]. As the site has not been archeologically investigated, it is not known why the stones were raised there [1]. Louisenlund was bought by King Frederik VII when he visited Bornholm in 1851 [1]. He named it after his mistress, Countess Louise Danner [1].
row.card: At Louisenlund, megaliths stand alone or in small groups, one of Denmark's largest collections. The site has not been archeologically investigated, so why they were raised is not known.

row.description: The Beckhampton Avenue was a curving prehistoric avenue of stones that ran broadly south west from Avebury towards The Longstones at Beckhampton in the English county of Wiltshire [1]. It probably dates to the late Neolithic and early Bronze Age [1]. Only one stone, known as "Adam", remains standing and even in William Stukeley's time there was little evidence on the surface of the avenue [1]. The other stones were probably broken up and sold by local landowners in the post-medieval era [1]. Excavations by the University of Southampton in 2000, however, revealed the parallel rows of holes that held the stones [1]. 120 metres of the avenue was uncovered and indicated that the avenue consisted of a double row of stones placed at 15 metres intervals in a similar pattern to those at Kennet Avenue [1]. Before the avenue was built, the site was host to an earlier Neolithic causewayed enclosure [1].
row.card: The Beckhampton Avenue curved from Avebury towards The Longstones, yet only one stone, called Adam, still stands. Excavations in 2000 revealed the parallel rows of holes that held them.

row.description: The so-called "Tomb of Absalom" is not only a burial structure in its own right, with its upper part serving as a nefesh (funeral monument) for the tomb in its lower part, but it was probably also meant as a nefesh for the adjacent burial cave system known as the "Cave" or "Tomb of Jehoshaphat", with which it forms one entity [1]. In 2003, a mid-4th-century inscription on one of the walls of the monument was discovered [1]. It reads, "This is the tomb of Zachariah, the martyr, the holy priest, the father of John" [1]. A second inscription of the same age discovered in 2003 says the monument is "the tomb of Simeon who was a very just man and a very devoted el(der) and (who was) waiting for the consolation of the people" [1]. The two inscriptions, discovered and deciphered by Joe Zias and Émile Puech, support the concept known from Byzantine period sources such as Theodosius (c. 530) that a tradition existed at the time, wrongly identifying the 1st-century monument as the tomb of James, the brother of Jesus; Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist; and Simeon [1].
row.card: Two inscriptions discovered in 2003 at Absalom's Tomb call the monument the tomb of Zachariah, the father of John, and the tomb of Simeon, who was a very just man.

row.description: The Ta' Ħaġrat temples in Mġarr, Malta are recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with several other Megalithic temples [1]. The larger Ta' Ħaġrat temple dates from the Ġgantija phase (3600–3200 BC); the smaller temple is dated to the Saflieni phase (3300–3000 BC) [1]. Ta' Ħaġrat is on the eastern outskirts of the village of Mġarr, roughly one kilometer from the Ta' Skorba temples [1]. The excavation of pottery deposits shows that a village stood on the site and predates the temples themselves [1]. This early pottery is dated to the Mġarr phase (3800-3600 BC) [1]. Ta' Ħaġrat is built out of lower coralline limestone, the oldest exposed rock in the Maltese Islands [1]. The complex contains two adjacent temples [1]. The site was excavated between 1923 and 1926 by Sir Temi Zammit, then Director of Museums [1].
row.card: On the eastern outskirts of Mġarr, the two adjacent Ta' Ħaġrat Temples stand on the site of a village that predates them. Sir Temi Zammit excavated the site between 1923 and 1926.

row.description: Federsee is a lake located just north of Bad Buchau in the region of Upper Swabia in Southern Germany [1]. It is surrounded by moorland, partially overgrown with reeds [1]. With a size of 33 km2, the area is one of the largest, groundwater fed, connected moorlands in Southern Germany [1]. At its deepest point, Lake Federsee has a depth of 2 metres [1]. The basin of Lake Federsee is famous for its excavations of Stone Age and Bronze Age artifacts [1].
row.card: Just north of Bad Buchau, the lake Federsee is surrounded by moorland, partially overgrown with reeds. Its basin is famous for excavations of Stone Age and Bronze Age artifacts.

row.description: The Bacho Kiro Cave is situated 5 km west of the town Dryanovo, Bulgaria, only 300 m away from the Dryanovo Monastery [1]. It is embedded in the canyons of the Andaka and Dryanovo River [1]. The cave is a four-storey labyrinth of galleries and corridors with a total length of 3,600 m [1]. The site has yielded the oldest human remains ever to be found in Bulgaria [1]. At one of the earliest known Aurignacian burials (layer 11), two pierced animal teeth were found and ordered into the distinct Bachokiran artifact assemblage [1]. Radiocarbon dated to over 43,000 years ago, they currently represent the oldest known ornaments in Europe [1]. With an approximate age of 46,000 years, human fossils consist of a pair of fragmented mandibles including at least one molar [1]. Whether these early humans were in fact Homo sapiens or Neanderthals was disputed until morphological analysis of a tooth and mitochondrial DNA of bone fragments established that remains were those of Homo sapiens [1].
row.card: Bacho Kiro Cave is a four-storey labyrinth of galleries and corridors, 3,600 m long in total. It yielded the oldest human remains ever found in Bulgaria, shown to be those of Homo sapiens.

row.description: The origin of the earliest settlement at the site of present-day Barcelona is unclear [1]. The ruins of an early settlement have been found, including different tombs and dwellings dating to earlier than 5000 BC [1]. Archeological evidence in the form of coins from the 3rd century BC have been found on the hills at the foot of Montjuïc with the name Bárkeno written in the Iberian script in the Iberian language [1]. In about 15 BC, the Romans redrew the town as a castrum centred on the "Mons Taber", a little hill near the Generalitat and city hall buildings [1]. The Roman Forum, at the crossing of the Cardo Maximus and Decumanus Maximus, was approximately placed where current Plaça de Sant Jaume is [1]. The city was conquered by the Visigoths in the early 5th century, becoming for a few years the capital of all Hispania [1].
row.card: How the earliest settlement at Barcelona began is unclear, but in about 15 BC the Romans redrew the town as a castrum centred on the Mons Taber, a little hill near the city hall.
